\section{Smart Compress Training Details}
\label{app:smart_compress_details}

The Smart Compress module is a cross-attention pooling layer inserted between SmolVLA's pixel-shuffle vision connector and the Qwen2-0.5B language backbone. It consists of $M$ learned query vectors that attend over the 128 vision tokens through standard multi-head cross-attention, producing $M$ compressed tokens as input to the LLM. The compressor adds 22.2M trainable parameters (approximately 5\% of SmolVLA's 451.5M total). Training is end-to-end: compressor and VLA policy parameters are jointly optimized.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Smart Compress training hyperparameters. Both $M=32$ and $M=64$ use identical procedures; only the number of query vectors differs.}
\label{tab:training_hyperparams}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Hyperparameter & Value \\
\midrule
Base checkpoint & SmolVLA LIBERO full-FT (100K steps) \\
Compressor parameters & 22.2M \\
Total training steps & 100,000 \\
Training duration & 6.5 hours (per configuration) \\
Training speed & 4.1 samples/sec \\
Seed & 42 \\
Dataset & HuggingFaceVLA/libero (130 task demos) \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{l}{\textit{$M=32$ final metrics}} \\
\quad Train action loss & 0.11 \\
\quad Eval action loss & 0.052 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{l}{\textit{$M=64$ final metrics}} \\
\quad Train action loss & 0.045 \\
\quad Eval action loss & 0.062 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The loss profile differs between configurations: $M=32$ has higher train loss (0.11 vs.\ 0.045) but lower eval loss (0.052 vs.\ 0.062), consistent with the smaller bottleneck acting as a stronger regularizer. Despite this loss difference, both achieve identical closed-loop success rates (61.6\%), reinforcing the finding that offline loss does not predict closed-loop performance (Section~\ref{sec:metric_disconnect}).


\section{Attention Entropy Measurement Details}
\label{app:entropy_details}

We measure the attention entropy ratio as the normalized Shannon entropy of the attention weights that the action decoder assigns to vision token positions. For a model with $N$ vision tokens, the entropy ratio is:
\begin{equation}
H_{\text{ratio}} = \frac{-\sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_i \log \alpha_i}{\log N}
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_i$ is the attention weight on the $i$-th vision token. The ratio ranges from 0 (all attention on one token) to 1 (uniform attention).

\paragraph{SmolVLA.} Measured on 2400 frames from LIBERO rollouts. The overall entropy ratio is 0.98, indicating near-uniform attention across all 128 vision tokens. The uniformity is consistent with the pixel-shuffle connector's output: because each token encodes 16 spatially contiguous patches via channel concatenation, all tokens are comparably information-dense, and the downstream LLM distributes attention accordingly.

\paragraph{OpenVLA.} Measured on 20 random images. The overall entropy ratio is 0.617. The layer-wise breakdown reveals progressive sharpening from shallow to deep layers:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item Shallow layers (1--4): 0.96--0.99
    \item Mid layers (12--20): 0.75--0.85
    \item Deep layers (24--30): 0.37--0.40 (minimum 0.371 at layer 28)
\end{itemize}
Only 9.3\% of total attention weight falls on vision tokens overall, and within that fraction, the distribution is highly non-uniform in deeper layers. This progressive concentration indicates that OpenVLA has learned to selectively attend to task-relevant spatial locations, a pattern enabled by the MLP projector's preservation of per-patch spatial granularity.

\paragraph{Measurement caveat.} The two measurements use different input distributions (2400 LIBERO rollout frames for SmolVLA vs.\ 20 random images for OpenVLA) and different sample sizes. The directional difference (0.98 vs.\ 0.617) is large enough to be robust to input variation, but a controlled comparison under identical input conditions is needed to confirm the exact magnitude.
